You must produce:
1. A BibTeX bibliography file (references.bib)
2. The full LaTeX paper (template.tex)

Instructions
• Use the research idea and experimental logs to construct a coherent, rigorous ML paper.
• For related work and baselines:
  – Search for and include influential papers published up until 2024-10.
  – Incorporate relevant literature and add the corresponding BibTeX entries to references.bib.
  – Do NOT hallucinate papers or reference keys; all citation entries must be real.
• In the LaTeX paper, cite papers using \cite{} with keys that match exactly with your entries in references.bib.
• Do not fabricate experimental results or make claims unsupported by the logs.

Materials
Here are all the raw research materials to assist with the writing process:

[RESEARCH IDEA]
## Problem Statement
Diffusion models have revolutionized generative modeling but suffer from slow sampling speeds due to the iterative nature of their reverse processes. While Consistency Models (CMs) address this by enabling single-step generation, they introduce a significant new bottleneck: training inefficiency. Current state-of-the-art methods for training CMs are exceptionally resource-intensive, often requiring orders of magnitude more compute than standard diffusion models or relying on complex distillation pipelines with frozen teacher networks.

Furthermore, training CMs from scratch is plagued by what we identify as the "curse of consistency." When naively optimizing for the consistency condition (where points on a trajectory map to the same origin), discretization errors accumulate, leading to training instability and slow convergence. We currently lack a training paradigm that combines the sampling speed of CMs with the training stability and efficiency of standard diffusion models.

## Core Hypothesis
We hypothesize that Diffusion Models (DMs) and Consistency Models (CMs) should not be treated as distinct model families, but rather as points on a continuum defined by the discretization of the sampling trajectory. specifically, we posit that a standard diffusion model is effectively a consistency model with a "loose" discretization (where the time step covers the entire trajectory).

Therefore, we believe we can efficiently train a Consistency Model by starting with a pretrained diffusion model and **smoothly interpolating** the training objective. By progressively tightening the consistency condition—starting from the standard diffusion objective and gradually shrinking the time intervals toward the differential limit—we can bypass the stability issues of training from scratch. This approach should allow us to "bootstrap" a pretrained diffusion model into a few-step consistency model with minimal computational overhead.

## Proposed Methodology (High-Level Technical Approach)

We propose a streamlined training scheme termed "Easy Consistency Tuning" (ECT). The methodology focuses on a continuous transition from diffusion behavior to consistency behavior.

**1. Unified Differential Perspective**
We will formulate the training objective based on a variable time gap, $\Delta t$, between two points on the noise trajectory.
*   **Initialization (Diffusion Mode):** At the beginning of the tuning phase, we will set $\Delta t$ to be large (effectively the distance from the current noise level to the clean data). In this state, the loss function mathematically resembles standard diffusion denoising. This allows us to initialize our network with weights from a standard pretrained diffusion model.
*   **Progressive Tightening:** We will introduce a time-dependent schedule that governs the sampling of the second point in the trajectory. Over the course of training iterations, we will gradually shrink $\Delta t$ towards zero.
*   **Target (Consistency Mode):** As $\Delta t$ approaches the differential limit, the objective transforms into the strict consistency condition (ensuring two infinitesimally close points map to the same output).

**2. Self-Contained Tuning**
Unlike traditional distillation which requires querying a heavy, frozen teacher model, our approach will use the model being trained (or its exponential moving average) to generate its own targets. By starting in "diffusion mode," the targets are initially stable (ground truth data), preventing the model from collapsing into trivial solutions early in training.

**3. Adaptive Gradient Weighting**
To ensure stability as the objective shifts, we will design a weighting function for the loss. The intuition is to normalize the gradient variance across different noise levels. Since predicting consistency for points far apart is harder than for points close together, adaptive weighting will prevent the loss from being dominated by high-error regions, facilitating a smooth handover from the diffusion objective to the consistency objective.

## Expected Contribution
*   **Theoretical Unification:** We aim to establish a theoretical framework where diffusion models are viewed as a special case of consistency models, simplifying the understanding of fast samplers.
*   **Training Efficiency:** We expect to demonstrate that this "pretraining + tuning" paradigm drastically reduces the computational resources (FLOPs and time) required to train state-of-the-art consistency models compared to training from scratch.
*   **Accessibility:** By removing the need for massive compute clusters or complex teacher-student pipelines, this method is intended to democratize access to high-quality, few-step generative models.
*   **Scalability:** We anticipate that this efficient tuning mechanism will adhere to power-law scaling, allowing future models to improve predictably with increased model size and compute.

[EXPERIMENTAL LOGS]
## 1. Experimental Setup

We evaluated the proposed method, Easy Consistency Tuning (ECT), and its resulting models (ECMs), against various diffusion and consistency model baselines. The experiments focused on training efficiency, generative sample quality, and scaling laws.

*   **Datasets:**
    *   **CIFAR-10:** Resolution $32 \times 32$. Evaluated in both unconditional and class-conditional settings.
    *   **ImageNet $64 \times 64$:** Class-conditional generation.
    *   **ImageNet $512 \times 512$:** Evaluated for latent space extension capabilities.
    *   **Swiss Roll (Toy Dataset):** Used for investigating adaptive weighting functions.

*   **Evaluation Metrics:**
    *   **FID (Fréchet Inception Distance):** Measured using 50k generated samples. Used to assess sample quality.
    *   **NFE (Number of Function Evaluations):** The number of model forward passes required to generate a sample (measure of sampling efficiency).
    *   **FD$_{DINOv2}$ (Fréchet Distance with DINOv2):** A metric using DINOv2-L features, considered to align better with human evaluation.
    *   **Training Cost:** Measured in GPU hours, total training images seen, or relative FLOPs.
    *   **Model Complexity:** Parameters (M) and FLOPs (G).

*   **Baselines Compared:**
    *   **Diffusion Models (DMs):** Score SDE, Score SDE-deep, EDM, EDM2-XL, ADM, PFGM++.
    *   **Diffusion Distillation:** PD (Progressive Distillation), GET, Diff-Instruct, TRACT, CD (Consistency Distillation), BOOT, DFNO, ECD (Easy Consistency Distillation - our variant).
    *   **Consistency Models (CMs):** iCT (Improved Consistency Training), iCT-deep.
    *   **GANs:** BigGAN, StyleGAN2-ADA, StyleGAN-XL.
    *   **Fast Samplers:** DPM-Solver-v3.

*   **Implementation Details:**
    *   **Architecture:** 
        *   CIFAR-10: Pretrained EDM of DDPM++ architecture.
        *   ImageNet $64 \times 64$: Pretrained EDM2 architecture (ranging from 280M to 1.1B parameters).
    *   **Optimization:**
        *   CIFAR-10: RAdam optimizer, $\beta=(0.9, 0.999)$, Learning rate $0.0001$. No decay/warmup.
        *   ImageNet $64 \times 64$: Adam optimizer, $\beta=(0.9, 0.99)$, inverse square root learning rate decay.
    *   **Training Schedule (ECT):** A continuous-time schedule shrinking $\Delta t \to 0$ using a mapping function $r/t = 1 - 1/q^{\lfloor \text{iters}/d \rfloor} n(t)$.
        *   CIFAR-10: $q=2$, $d=$ total_iters//8.
        *   ImageNet: $q=4$, $d=$ total_iters//4.
    *   **Dropout:** High dropout rates were found beneficial. 
        *   CIFAR-10: 20% (FID evaluation), 30% (FD$_{DINOv2}$ evaluation).
        *   ImageNet $64 \times 64$: 40% (ECM-S), 50% (ECM-M/L/XL).
    *   **Hardware:** NVIDIA A6000 (CIFAR), NVIDIA H100 (ImageNet scaling), NVIDIA A100 (1-hour prototyping).
    *   **Iterations:** Typically 100k iterations for tuning, with variations (200k, 400k) for scaling analysis.

## 3. Qualitative Observations

**Model Training & Efficiency:**
*   Observation: Training a state-of-the-art CM on CIFAR-10 typically takes one week on 8 GPUs; ECT reduced this significantly.
*   Observation: ECT achieved 2-step FID of 2.73 on CIFAR-10 within 1 hour on a single A100 GPU.
*   Observation: Total cost of pretraining + tuning for ECT was approximately $1/4$ to $1/3$ of the FLOPs used by iCT.
*   Observation: The tuning stage specifically accounted for 10% or less of the overall cost.
*   Observation: On ImageNet 64x64, ECT rivals iCT-deep using $1/4$ of the overall compute and $1/2$ the model size.
*   Observation: 2-step ECM fine-tuned for 100k iterations matched Score SDE-deep (which has 2x model depth) in FID while using 2000x fewer steps (2 vs 2000).

**Scaling Laws (Figures 3 & 4):**
*   Observation: ECT obeys classic power law scaling for model size, FLOPs, and training compute.
*   Observation: Scaling up training compute showed a power-law decay in FD$_{DINOv2}$.
*   Observation: The correlation between log(Training Compute) and log(FD$_{DINOv2}$) was -0.9940 for 1-step and -0.9996 for 2-step generation.
*   Observation: Power law fit for 1-step: $FD_{DINOv2} = 263 \cdot C^{-0.060}$.
*   Observation: Power law fit for 2-step: $FD_{DINOv2} = 164 \cdot C^{-0.028}$.
*   Observation: Both 1-step and 2-step generation exhibited log-linear scaling for model FLOPs and parameters.
*   Observation: There is an inference "sweet spot" where 2-step inference of smaller models (e.g., 498M ECM-M) outperformed 1-step inference of larger models (e.g., 1.1B ECM-XL).

**Convergence and Stability ("Curse of Consistency" - Figure 1):**
*   Observation: Training with a fixed small $\Delta t$ leads to slower convergence and instability as $\Delta t \to 0$ (number of intervals $N \to \infty$).
*   Observation: A tradeoff exists where decreasing $\Delta t$ makes single-step prediction easier but error accumulation ($N \times e_{max}$) potentially worse.
*   Observation: Shrinking $\Delta t \to 0$ gradually during training (ECT schedule) resulted in better final performance than starting with $\Delta t \approx dt$.

**Design Choices (Ablations):**
*   Observation: **Dropout:** CMs benefit from significantly higher dropout rates than DMs. Increasing dropout from 0.10 to 0.40 on ImageNet 64x64 improved 2-step FID from 4.53 to 3.24.
*   Observation: **Pretraining:** Initializing from a pretrained DM significantly improved performance compared to training from scratch (FD$_{DINOv2}$ 190.13 vs 242.30).
*   Observation: **Weighting:** Adaptive weighting based on prediction error magnitude ($w(\Delta)$) improved performance by controlling gradient variance.
*   Observation: Insights from tuning (e.g., adaptive weighting) transferred back to improve the pretraining stage itself (EDM pretrained with ECT recipe converged 2x faster).

**Continuous Time Schedule:**
*   Observation: Using a mapping function that gradually shrinks $\Delta t$ improved training stability compared to fixed schedules.
*   Observation: Setting $r/t \approx 0.99$ immediately (no shrink) led to divergence on ImageNet 64x64.

Role: Senior AI Researcher and Academic Writer.
Objective: Complete a machine learning research paper by filling in missing sections of a provided LaTeX template and generating a corresponding bibliography file. You must produce a scientifically sound, well-structured paper suitable for submission to a top-tier ML conference.

Inputs
You will receive the following materials:
• idea.md: Detailed description of the proposed method and technical ideas.
• experimental_log.md: Raw experimental results and observations used to construct tables, figures, and analysis.
• conference_guidelines.md: Formatting and stylistic requirements for the target conference.
• figures_list: A list of figures that may be referenced in the paper.

Conference Guidelines
# ICLR 2025 Paper Writing Guidelines

Below are the instructions to help you with the LaTeX paper writing process for ICLR 2025.

## General Setup
* **Document Class:** `\documentclass{article}`
* **Required Packages:**
    ```latex
    \usepackage{iclr2025_conference,times}
    \usepackage{hyperref}
    \usepackage{url}
    % Optional but recommended for math
    \input{math_commands.tex}
    ```
* **Style Files:** You must use `iclr2025_conference.sty` and `iclr2025_conference.bst`.

## Anonymity (Crucial)
* ICLR is double-blind. **Do not** include real author names or affiliations in the submission version, use "Ambitious AI Researcher" instead.
* Use the third person when citing your own prior work (e.g., "Earlier work by Smalle (2024)..." instead of "In our earlier work...").
* You may post your paper on arXiv, but do not explicitly refer to the arXiv version in the paper to maintain anonymity.

## Paper Length
* **Main Text:** Strict upper limit of **10 pages**.
* **Citations:** Unlimited additional pages.
* **Ethics & Reproducibility Statements:** Optional. Do not count toward the page limit (max 1 page each).
* **Acknowledgments:** Do not count toward the page limit.

## Abstract
The abstract must be limited to **one paragraph**.
* **Margins:** Indented 1/2 inch (3 picas) on both left and right-hand margins.
* **Font:** 10-point type, vertical spacing of 11-points.
* **Title:** The word `\textsc{Abstract}` must be centered, in small caps, and in point size 12.
* **Spacing:** Two line spaces precede the abstract.

## Formatting Your Paper
The text must be confined within a rectangle 5.5 inches (33 picas) wide and 9 inches (54 picas) long. The left margin is 1.5 inch (9 picas).
* **Font:** Times New Roman (via `times` package) is preferred.
* **Size:** 10-point type with 11-point vertical spacing.
* **Paragraphs:** Separated by 1/2 line space, with **no indentation**.
* **Paper Title:** 17-point, small caps, left-aligned.

### Headings
* **First Level:** Small caps (`\textsc`), flush left, 12-point. One line space before, 1/2 after.

references.text:
## Problem Statement

Diffusion Models (DMs) have achieved dominance in visual content generation, but their reliance on iteratively solving a stochastic differential equation (SDE) or probability flow ODE (PF-ODE) necessitates hundreds of function evaluations per sample, resulting in slow inference speeds. Consistency Models (CMs) address this by enforcing a property where all points on a sampling trajectory map to the same initial data point, enabling 1-step generation. However, training CMs is currently plagued by high resource intensity and instability.

We identify this instability as the "Curse of Consistency." Theoretically, the consistency condition requires the time derivative of the consistency function to be zero ($\frac{df}{dt} = 0$). In practice, training approximates this via finite differences over time intervals $\Delta t$. When $\Delta t \to 0$ (approximating the true differential), error accumulation across the trajectory diverges, making optimization unstable. Conversely, large $\Delta t$ stabilizes training but fails to capture the differential consistency required for high-quality 1-step sampling. Current solutions, such as Consistency Distillation (CD) or improved Consistency Training (iCT), rely on computationally expensive teachers, complex discrete time schedules, or perceptual loss metrics (LPIPS) that introduce bias. There is a lack of a unified, efficient training framework that can transition a model from a stable diffusion objective to a strict consistency objective without the massive computational overhead currently required.

## Core Hypothesis

We propose **Easy Consistency Tuning (ECT)**, a training paradigm based on the hypothesis that Diffusion Models are merely a special case of Consistency Models where the discretization interval is maximal ($\Delta t = t$). By viewing the generative process through a differential equation lens, we hypothesize that we can stabilize CM training by smoothly interpolating the training objective.

Instead of training from scratch with a fixed discrete schedule, we will initialize a consistency model from a pre-trained diffusion model (or pre-train one as a first stage). We will then employ a **continuous-time training schedule** that progressively tightens the consistency condition. By initializing with $\Delta t \approx t$ (standard diffusion denoising) and gradually annealing the interval such that $\Delta t \to 0$ (differential consistency) over the course of training, we believe we can mitigate the "Curse of Consistency." This approach should allow us to train high-quality, 1-step generative models with a fraction of the computational resources of iCT or CD, without requiring frozen teacher models or auxiliary perceptual losses.

## Proposed Methodology (Detailed Technical Approach)

We will construct a framework that unifies diffusion and consistency training into a single continuous process. This involves a specific mathematical formulation of the consistency condition, a novel time-sampling scheduler, and an adaptive weighting mechanism.

### 1. Mathematical Formulation and Boundary Conditions
We build upon the Probability Flow ODE (PF-ODE) defined as:
$$ \frac{\mathrm{d}\mathbf{x}_t}{\mathrm{d}t} = -t \nabla_{\mathbf{x}_t} \log p_t(\mathbf{x}_t) $$
where $t$ represents the noise level. Our model will learn a consistency function $f_\theta(\mathbf{x}_t, t)$ that maps any point $\mathbf{x}_t$ on the trajectory to the origin $\mathbf{x}_0$. The core consistency condition we aim to enforce is:
$$ f(\mathbf{x}_t, t) = \mathbf{x}_0 \iff \frac{\mathrm{d}f}{\mathrm{d}t} = 0, \quad f(\mathbf{x}_0, 0) = \mathbf{x}_0 $$
To strictly enforce the boundary condition at $t=0$, we will parameterize the network $f_\theta$ using skip connections:
$$ f_\theta(\mathbf{x}_t, t) = c_{\mathrm{skip}}(t)\mathbf{x}_t + c_{\mathrm{out}}(t)F_\theta(\mathbf{x}_t, t) $$
We will define $c_{\mathrm{skip}}(0) = 1$ and $c_{\mathrm{out}}(0) = 0$.

### 2. Continuous-Time Training Schedule
The core of ECT is the dynamic selection of the time intervals used for the finite-difference approximation of the time derivative. For a given noise level $t$, we must select a secondary time point $r < t$.

We define the approximation gap $\Delta t = t - r$.
*   **Stage 1 (Diffusion Pretraining):** We set $r=0$. The objective becomes $\| f_\theta(\mathbf{x}_t) - \mathbf{x}_0 \|$, which is identical to standard diffusion training.
*   **Stage 2 (Consistency Tuning):** We progressively shrink $\Delta t \to 0$ by adjusting $r$ relative to $t$.

We will implement a parameterized mapping function $p(r | t, \text{iters})$ to control this progression. We define the ratio $r/t$ as:
$$ \frac{r}{t} = 1 - \frac{1}{q^{\lfloor \text{iters}/d \rfloor}} n(t) $$
Here:
*   $\text{iters}$ is the current training iteration.
*   $q > 1$ and $d$ are hyperparameters controlling the annealing rate (how fast $\Delta t \to 0$).
*   $n(t)$ is a non-linear adjustment function to balance difficulty across noise levels.

We define $n(t)$ using a sigmoid-based scaling to handle gradient imbalances at small vs. large $t$:
$$ n(t) = 1 + \frac{k}{1 + e^{bt}} $$
where $k$ and $b$ are scalar constants (e.g., $k=8, b=1$). We will strictly enforce $r \ge 0$. This schedule ensures that early in training, the model stabilizes via global denoising ($r \approx 0$), and gradually shifts focus to local consistency ($\mathbf{x}_t \to \mathbf{x}_{t-\epsilon}$).

### 3. Loss Function and Adaptive Weighting
We will optimize the model parameters $\theta$ using a consistency loss with a stop-gradient operator on the target:
$$ \mathcal{L}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{x}_0, \epsilon, t} \left[ w(t, r) \cdot \mathbf{d}\left( f_\theta(\mathbf{x}_t), f_{\text{sg}(\theta)}(\mathbf{x}_r) \right) \right] $$
where $\mathbf{x}_t = \mathbf{x}_0 + t\epsilon$, $\mathbf{x}_r = \mathbf{x}_0 + r\epsilon$, and $\text{sg}(\cdot)$ stops gradient backpropagation.

Crucially, we will implement an **Adaptive Weighting** function $w(t, r)$ to control gradient variance. We decompose the weight into a time-dependent term $\bar{w}(t)$ and an error-dependent term $w(\Delta)$:
$$ w(t) = \bar{w}(t) \cdot w(\Delta) = \bar{w}(t) \cdot \frac{1}{(\| \Delta \|_2^2 + c^2)^p} $$
where:
*   $\Delta = f_\theta(\mathbf{x}_t) - f_{\text{sg}(\theta)}(\mathbf{x}_r)$ is the prediction error.
*   $c$ is a small smoothing constant.
*   $p$ controls the strength of the weighting (e.g., $p=0.5$ approximates Pseudo-Huber properties).

This formulation allows the loss to adapt on a per-sample basis, preventing outliers from destabilizing the trajectory matching when $\Delta t$ becomes small.

### 4. Algorithm Construction
The complete training loop will proceed as follows:
1.  Initialize $\theta$ from a pre-trained diffusion model (or random initialization for full pipeline).
2.  Sample $\mathbf{x}_0 \sim p_{\text{data}}$, $\epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}, \mathbf{I})$, and $t \sim p(t)$ (LogNormal).
3.  Compute $r$ using the iteration-dependent mapping function defined above.
4.  Generate perturbed inputs $\mathbf{x}_t$ and $\mathbf{x}_r$.
5.  Compute the consistency loss with adaptive weighting.
6.  Update $\theta$ via stochastic gradient descent until $\Delta t \to 0$ convergence is reached.

## Expected Contribution

1.  **Unified Framework:** We expect to establish a theoretical and practical continuum between Diffusion Models and Consistency Models, proving that diffusion training is simply consistency training with maximal discretization.
2.  **Efficiency:** We anticipate that ECT will reduce the computational cost of training state-of-the-art 1-step generative models by a factor of 3x to 4x compared to current best practices (iCT), by removing the need for auxiliary teachers and enabling faster convergence.
3.  **Scalability:** By mitigating the "Curse of Consistency" through continuous annealing, we expect this method to adhere to power-law scaling, allowing Consistency Models to efficiently scale to larger architectures and datasets where previous methods became unstable or prohibitively expensive.

preinstalled.en: orchestrator image: upstream code at the pin (unmodified), uv-locked dependencies, the docker CLI (a shim adds proxy and CA to sibling containers); agent image: upstream's own agent-cli Dockerfile

notes.benchmark_paths: A benchmark item's paths are mounted into the agent containers unless upstream mounts the same path itself (/workspace and below, /home/agent-home, /task-source, /run, /tmp): those are left out and listed in logs/sibling-mounts.txt. The agents work in upstream's own /workspace (the run directory), so a deliverable the official prompt names under such a path is not written where the run collects it.
notes.venue: paper.paper_format=iclr for every task. The system has only iclr and alife specs and does not choose a venue itself; ICML and NeurIPS templates and a system-chosen venue are unsupported.
notes.task_input: Only the `# Goal` and `# Rubrics` sections of task.md are read: all five candidate files are put under `# Goal` with their headings turned into bold lines; `# Rubrics` carries a neutral line. The paradigm is optimisation of a scalar score: the task-drafting phase (documented as experimental) turns the brief into an evaluator and a seed program.
notes.phases: execution.phases=task_drafting,investigation,final_evaluation,paper; the system's own default also runs ablations and posthoc; final_evaluation stays because a drafted task requires it before the paper. review/revision (second model) are never selected.
notes.agent_pool: agent.pool and agent.models.* are left empty: one model for every phase.
notes.second_provider: No OPENAI/GEMINI key is supplied (concept figures stay in deterministic export mode).
notes.time: No global wall-clock or token cap exists upstream; the runner enforces time_limit_hours. Native caps used: idea cycles=3, per-phase timeouts from [systems.agentic-scientist].
notes.network: Sibling agent containers run on the shield's internal network; the agents keep their CLI WebFetch/Bash network, which go through the shield. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield.

preinstalled.zh: python:3.11 bookworm；上游代码按 PYTHONPATH 使用；pdflatex + bibtex；CPU 版 PyTorch 和 numpy、scipy、scikit-learn、pandas、matplotlib 等（constraints.txt 固定）
preinstalled.en: python:3.11 bookworm; upstream code via PYTHONPATH; pdflatex + bibtex; CPU PyTorch with numpy, scipy, scikit-learn, pandas, matplotlib and more (pinned by constraints.txt)

notes.model: claude-opus-5-5 through the Anthropic Messages API (llm.provider=anthropic), no fallback models, reviewer model = same model. Requests carry model, messages and max_tokens only (no tools, no thinking parameter); ARC's per-stage temperature is not sent because the model rejects it, so the API default applies.
notes.agent: ARC is not a tool-using coding agent: its 23-stage pipeline, its own code agent and its reviewers are prompt chains over plain chat completions. conditions.agent=claude means only that the provider is Anthropic; Claude Code is not involved. Generated experiments run as a plain subprocess in the container.
notes.effort: ARC has no effort setting; usage-log.patch sends output_config.effort='high' with every request. Haiku 5.5 thinks by default and ARC's per-stage max_tokens (for example 4096) is shared with the thinking tokens, so long outputs can still be cut short.
notes.venue: Not chosen by the system: export.target_conference=iclr_2026 comes from [systems.autoresearchclaw].
notes.tokens: ARC records no usage. A logging-only patch (usage-log.patch) appends each Messages API `usage` block to anthropic-usage.jsonl; cost is not computed. The same patch carries the RWE_OMIT_TEMPERATURE and RWE_EFFORT switches.
notes.time: No global wall-clock or budget cap in ARC; only the runner's limit applies. Per experiment run 3600 s, refinement iterations 10, repair cycles 3.
notes.input: Chinese pack text goes verbatim (candidate files concatenated, with <!-- file --> markers) into prompts.extra_prompts of 18 stages. ARC takes one topic string and checks generated code against it, so research.topic is the candidate TASK.md verbatim with whitespace collapsed. Literature queries come from the stage-3 model plan; ARC's ASCII keyword splitter and its whitespace-based query expansion yield a few useless queries from the Chinese text. Starter papers are guidance text only: ARC cannot ingest seed papers.
notes.search: Web search, crawling, GitHub, HF Hub, Gemini and OpenCode are off. Literature search in stage 4 uses ['openalex', 'semantic_scholar'] through ARC's own clients behind the shield proxy; stages 8, 17, 22 and 23 (novelty, citation verification) always also query arXiv, CrossRef and DataCite; the shield date-bounds those API calls like the others (a late DOI answers 403).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: every request to api.anthropic.com is built in researchclaw/llm/anthropic_adapter.py:136-148 and carries only model, messages, max_tokens, optional temperature, output_config.effort and system, never a tools or web_search field; the OpenAI-compatible client (OpenRouter :online / plugins) is not used (llm.provider=anthropic), web_search.enabled=false, Gemini is only used by the disabled figure_agent.nano_banana. Provider hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so such a path would be invisible to the audit.
notes.secrets: Generated experiment code inherits the container environment, including the API keys (ARC offers no switch to scrub it).
notes.profile: project.profile=ml_generic is fixed for all tasks; research.domains is left empty because the literature screen rejects papers outside the stated domain (a theory task failed with domains=[machine-learning]).

preinstalled.zh: 上游锁定依赖（uv sync --frozen）加兼容补丁 compat.patch；TeX Live（含 fonts-extra、latexmk）；给 agent 用的研究 Python 环境 /opt/research
preinstalled.en: upstream's locked dependencies (uv sync --frozen) plus compat.patch; TeX Live (with fonts-extra and latexmk); a research Python environment for the agent in /opt/research

notes.agent: No external coding agent: EvoScientist runs its own in-process planner/research/code/debug/writing sub-agents (LangChain deepagents) on the one configured model. conditions.agent only selects the provider; Claude Code and Codex are not used.
notes.model: Main agent, sub-agents and EvoScientist's auxiliary calls (tool selector, memory workers, summariser, graders) all use the configured model; auxiliary_model and model_fallbacks are empty.
notes.effort: Upstream hard-wires effort=max and max_tokens=128000 for Anthropic models. compat.patch makes the effort come from EVOSCIENTIST_REASONING_EFFORT (= conditions.effort); max_tokens stays 128000 (a cap, not a cost driver). Adaptive thinking (display=summarized) is upstream and not switchable.
notes.paper: The core writes a Markdown report (final_report.md); the EvoSkills paper-writing skill gives a generic LaTeX `article` skeleton with no ICML/ICLR/NeurIPS style and no compile step. The image has TeX Live (latexmk, fonts-extra) but no venue style files; the task asks for an official template, so a venue-formatted PDF depends on the agent obtaining the style through the shield. No extra pipeline stage was added; absent items are listed in result.missing.
notes.tools: skill_manager (git clone of any repository as a skill) is not registered (compat.patch); the Tavily key is not set so tavily_search does not exist; LANGGRAPH_CLI_NO_ANALYTICS=1; EvoSkills is baked in at its pinned commit. The execute shell and the EvoSkills paper-navigator scripts reach the world only through the shield; S2_DATE_CUTOFF is not set (the shield bounds dates).
notes.server_side_search: Not reachable: EvoScientist binds no provider-side search tool to any model (its only tools are think_tool, tavily_search when TAVILY_API_KEY is set, MCP tools from mcp.yaml, deepagents built-ins and skills; EvoScientist/EvoScientist.py:671-672 and 754-755 at the pin; the one bind_tools call is the tool selector's own output schema, middleware/tool_selector.py:166). TAVILY_API_KEY is not passed and the image has no mcp.yaml, so no search tool exists. Anthropic/OpenAI hosts are only tunnelled by the shield, so a provider-side search would be invisible to the audit.
notes.credentials: The provider key is in the process environment and EvoScientist's execute shell inherits the environment (upstream has no switch); the key is therefore visible to the agent's shell. It is a run-scoped copy and is not logged by this adapter.
notes.memory: A fresh data dir per run (baked skills, empty memory). Memory workers, skill synthesis and the scheduler stay at upstream defaults, so their LLM calls count in the usage log.
notes.limits: async sub-agents off (README advice for scripted runs); recursion_limit=1000000; model retry wait in auto-mode 1800 s (time without progress counts as wall time); execute timeout 300 s per command. No token or cost budget exists.
